<<Turbulence Over Europe: The EasyJet Brexit Story>>

Section 1  
EasyJet entered the new financial year with the strange feeling of having broken records while nursing a bruise. Profits had fallen 17%, slipping from £494m to £408m, even as the airline flew 80.2 million passengers, almost 10% more than the year before. The departure halls at Gatwick and other hubs were never quiet; orange uniforms threaded through crowds, boarding gates opened and closed in quick succession, and planes left their stands with barely an empty seat. Yet beneath the surface, the plunge in the pound after the Brexit vote had quietly eaten more than £100m from the airline’s earnings. Fuel, leases, maintenance – all those dollar-priced essentials that kept jets in the sky became more expensive the moment sterling stumbled.

Section 2  
Carolyn McCall, the chief executive, stood by a glass wall in the Luton headquarters, watching the grey midday light lean against the office tower that housed the airline’s operations. Her team had chosen a clear strategy years earlier: be number one or two in Europe’s leading airports, treat passengers with friendly and efficient service, and shave away any unnecessary cost without sacrificing safety. In an aviation society shaken by bankruptcies and carriers cancelling routes at short notice, that strategy now looked almost like a dare: grow while others retrenched, invest while rivals hesitated. EasyJet’s orange tails continued to line up on European tarmacs even as smaller airlines vanished from departure boards, freeing up precious airport slots and pushing some fares higher again.

Section 3  
Yet Brexit hovered over every meeting agenda and every spreadsheet. To keep full access to European skies after 2019, the airline needed to show it was majority owned and controlled by EU nationals. About a third of the shares were held by founder Stelios Haji-Ioannou, whose UK-Cypriot status meant his stake still qualified. The rest, however, resembled a restless shoal, with many investors based in the UK and others spread across the continent like fishing boats along a jagged coast. At the 2018 AGM, directors planned to ask for new powers to force some UK shareholders to sell if the balance of ownership ever tipped the wrong way – a technical fix, McCall insisted, but one that hinted at the new fragility of cross-border business. On the morning the results were announced, the market offered a small reward: shares rose more than 5% as traders seized on strong forward bookings and improving revenues, a reminder that even in turbulent political weather, demand for travel – for holidays, reunions, negotiations and new ventures – remained stubbornly strong.
